oneSentence: The ability of systems or organisations to exchange information and use it correctly under compatible rules.
plainExplanation:
Interoperability means separate systems can work together without people having to rebuild or retype everything each time. What goes in can be data, documents, messages, technical formats or agreed procedures. What happens in the middle is that the parts match well enough to exchange and interpret that input. What comes out is coordinated work across tools, teams or institutions.

This idea applies at more than one level. Technical interoperability is about compatible file formats, interfaces and data structures. Organisational interoperability is about workflows, roles and responsibilities lining up. Legal or policy interoperability is about rules that allow exchange and use under agreed conditions. A system may succeed at one level and fail at another.

In AI governance, the term often appears when countries, agencies or platforms need to share information about AI systems, risks, audits or standards-based assessments. For example, one body may record an incident in one format and another body may need to compare it with its own records. If the categories, definitions and metadata are aligned, the information can travel and still keep its meaning.

Interoperability is often confused with standardisation, but they are not the same. A standard is a documented specification or agreed method. Interoperability is the practical ability to connect and use information across boundaries. Standards can help create interoperability, but systems can follow a standard and still fail to work together if implementation, governance or context differ.

everydayAnalogy.title: A parcel changing couriers
everydayAnalogy.story: A parcel may travel through several delivery companies. Interoperability means each company can scan the label, interpret the address and handling codes in the same way, and update the delivery record under compatible rules. If every scanner reads the barcode but one courier treats “keep upright” as “deliver urgently”, the systems exchange data but do not use it correctly.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A report template is a simple object, but real interoperability often involves many moving parts at once: software interfaces, identifiers, permissions, legal constraints and different definitions. Two systems may exchange a file successfully yet still not be truly interoperable if they classify the same event differently, apply different access rules or lose important context during transfer.

visual.title: How interoperability turns separate systems into usable exchange
visual.learningObjective: Show that interoperability requires not just transfer, but also shared meaning and usable action across systems.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow with four stages. Stage 1 shows two separate systems with different internal formats. Stage 2 shows a bridge layer with shared fields, identifiers and rules. Stage 3 shows exchanged data being interpreted correctly. Stage 4 shows a joint output such as a combined dashboard or report. Read from left to right to see that simple transfer is not enough; the receiving side must preserve meaning and use the information.

steps.label: Separate systems
steps.explanation: Two organisations collect similar information, but they store it differently.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw two boxes labelled System A and System B. Inside each, show different field names for similar concepts, such as 'incident_date' in one and 'date of event' in the other.

steps.label: Shared bridge
steps.explanation: They agree on mappings, formats, identifiers and rules for exchange.
steps.visualInstruction: Place a middle layer between the systems labelled Shared schema, metadata and exchange rules. Add arrows from both systems into this layer.

steps.label: Correct interpretation
steps.explanation: When information moves across, the receiving side can place each item in the right category and keep its meaning.
steps.visualInstruction: Show an arrow from the bridge to a receiving box where fields line up correctly: date to date, location to location, category to category.

steps.label: Usable joint output
steps.explanation: Because the data can be exchanged and interpreted, people can compare, combine or act on it more reliably.
steps.visualInstruction: End with a combined output panel showing a simple chart, alert list or merged report built from both sources.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each stage to reveal one extra note: format, meaning, governance, then outcome.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram is a four-stage flow from left to right. First, two separate systems hold similar information in different structures. Second, a shared bridge layer aligns fields, metadata, identifiers and exchange rules. Third, data passes through that bridge and is interpreted correctly by the receiving system, so categories and dates still mean the same thing after transfer. Fourth, the aligned information is used in a combined output such as a merged report or dashboard. The main lesson is that interoperability is more than sending data; the receiver must also preserve meaning and be able to use it.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static four-column diagram shows separate systems, then a shared bridge, then correct interpretation, then a joint output, with labels explaining that transfer alone does not guarantee interoperability.

workedExample.scenario: A programme officer in a regional bureau must combine country office progress reports in the corporate portal before the reporting window closes.
workedExample.input: One office reports activities by workplan output, another by project code, and a third by results-framework indicator. Their exports also represent reporting periods and implementation status differently.
process: The programme officer identifies which fields are technically exchangeable and maps each local field to the portal structure.
The reporting focal points agree common definitions for reporting period, completion status and responsible office. A shared label without a shared meaning would merely produce tidier confusion.
A conversion rule changes the files into the required structure while retaining source identifiers and flagging entries that do not map cleanly.
The offices review the flagged entries and confirm the applicable clearance and access rules before upload.
workedExample.result: The portal can combine and display the reports without changing their intended meaning. Entries that remain ambiguous are held for manual review rather than silently assigned to the wrong result.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A gender adviser in a UN Country Team working group is consolidating agency inputs for the situation report before the regional bulletin closes. The source systems export compatible spreadsheets, but they use different definitions for age groups, referral status and reporting periods.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: Interoperability requires more than files that open. The working group must align field formats, definitions, metadata, clearance steps and access rules so that each contribution is interpreted and used as intended.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Use only aggregated, appropriately cleared information. Do not enter respondent-level, survivor, witness or other protection-sensitive data into an external tool that has not been approved for it. Combining datasets can expose identities through linked attributes even when names have been removed.

whyItMatters: For non-specialists, interoperability matters because many policy and operational failures come from systems that cannot share usable information. That can mean duplicate work, delayed analysis, inconsistent oversight and poor comparisons across organisations or countries. In AI governance, it affects whether audit results, incident reports, risk classifications and technical documentation can be reused across borders and institutions. Good interoperability can lower costs and support coordination, but weak interoperability can create false confidence if data moves without preserving meaning, context or safeguards.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If two systems can send files to each other, they are interoperable.
commonMisconceptions.correction: File transfer is only one part. True interoperability also requires the receiving side to interpret the information correctly and use it in a meaningful workflow. If categories, identifiers or definitions do not match, the exchange may succeed technically but fail in practice.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Interoperability simply means using one international standard everywhere.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Standards often help, but interoperability is broader. It depends on implementation choices, governance, legal permissions, metadata and shared definitions. Two organisations may use the same standard and still not work together well, or they may achieve partial interoperability through mappings between different standards.

Not always. Greater connectivity can increase privacy, security and governance risks if it enables inappropriate sharing or unclear responsibility. Good design sets limits on what is exchanged, who can access it and for what purpose.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Different systems or organisations can share information and use it properly, instead of forcing people to re-enter or reinterpret everything by hand.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Interoperability is the capacity of heterogeneous systems, institutions or regulatory arrangements to exchange data, messages or artefacts and preserve sufficient semantic consistency, procedural alignment and governance compatibility for the receiving party to use them as intended. It can include syntactic compatibility, such as common file formats or APIs; semantic compatibility, meaning shared definitions and metadata; organisational compatibility, such as aligned workflows and responsibilities; and legal compatibility, including lawful bases, access conditions and accountability arrangements. It is therefore an outcome across layers, not just a feature of one technical interface.

keyTakeaway: Interoperability means systems can exchange information and preserve enough shared format, meaning, process and governance for it to be used correctly.

quickCheck.question: Which situation best shows interoperability rather than simple data transfer?
options: Two agencies email each other spreadsheets, but each must manually recode the categories before analysis.
A platform exports files in a common format, and another system imports them into matching fields with shared definitions and access rules.
One ministry requires all staff to use the same brand of software on every computer.
A team stores reports as PDF images so every office sees the same page layout.
quickCheck.explanation: The key test is not whether data moves, but whether it arrives in a form the receiving side can interpret and use correctly. Shared format, definitions and rules make that possible. The other options either still require manual repair or confuse interoperability with uniformity.

contested: The core idea is widely used, but the exact scope can vary by context: some communities stress technical compatibility, while others include organisational, legal and semantic alignment as essential parts.

issues.problem: The definition makes “rules” a subject that can exchange and use information. Rules can enable or constrain interoperability, but they do not themselves exchange information.
issues.fix: The ability of systems or organisations to exchange information and use it correctly under compatible rules.

issues.problem: The example treats “country” and “state” as equivalent fields without establishing that they describe the same geographic level. “State” may refer to a subnational area, so this mapping could silently corrupt the data. The next step then incorrectly applies a shared country list to both fields.
issues.fix: Replace the two steps with: “They map IDs, dates, system types and severity, but verify whether country and state describe the same geography.” and “They agree dates use YYYY-MM-DD, locations use one shared geographic classification, and severity uses the same four levels.”

issues.problem: The totals do not compute. There are 120 + 95 = 215 records. If 11 require manual review, 215 - 11 = 204 are directly comparable, as the process states. The result accounts for 62 + 41 = 103 comparable cases, then says “the rest” require manual review. That would make 215 - 103 = 112 records require review, not 11. Alternatively, among the 204 comparable records, 204 - 103 = 101 remain unaccounted for.
issues.fix: The agencies produce one summary table: 62 comparable cases involve verification errors, 41 involve identification errors, 101 involve other aligned categories, and 11 require manual review.

issues.problem: The blanket statement about the other options is incomplete. The PDF option is neither manual repair nor uniformity. It shows consistent display, but does not demonstrate that information can be reused across systems with shared meaning.
issues.fix: Option 2 combines transfer with matching fields, shared definitions and access rules. Option 1 needs manual recoding. Option 3 shows uniformity, not exchange. Option 4 shows consistent display, not cross-system reuse.
